source.title: A unifying framework from neural superposition to sparse interpretable codes
source.authors: David A. Klindt; Charles O'Neill; P. Reizinger; Harald Maurer; N. Miolane

record.file_problem: The supplied full text is titled “From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks,” while the provided metadata gives a different title. The text identifies itself as arXiv:2503.01824v1; it appears to be a title/version discrepancy, not an unrelated document.
record.tranche_reason: The paper presents a theoretical perspective on superposition, sparse coding and interpretability. It does not test cross-model representational alignment, convergence across seeds, or any other listed claim version; its relevant examples test additivity within one vision model.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports an additivity analysis in ViT-B/16, including an aggregate result over N = 10 further examples. This is a related but different construct from similarity between independently trained models. Statements about convergence of sparse codes across networks and other empirical findings are attributed to cited work and are not recorded as this study’s results.
record.test_reason: A perspective paper on superposition, identifiability and sparse coding. Its only own result is a within-model additivity check in ViT-B/16 (Fig. 1). It has no cross-model, cross-seed or cross-modal similarity measurement. Statements about sparse codes converging across networks (Lan et al., Chen and Bonner) and SAE features not being universal (Paulo and Belrose) are cited, not tested. It mentions the Platonic hypothesis (Huh et al.) only as an analogy for its data-generating-process assumption.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors argue three things: classification-trained networks invert the data-generating process up to a linear map (a cited theorem); compressed sensing and sparse coding can lift features out of superposition; and quantitative interpretability metrics are needed to evaluate them. They note limits: SAEs recover codes suboptimally, binding is unresolved, and behaviour under distribution shift is unknown. They also cite, without testing, evidence that sparse codes from different networks converge.
record.recipe_differences: The study gives a theoretical perspective and an illustrative within-model additivity analysis; it does not apply the original cross-model similarity-and-scale approach.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported additivity result differs between neural representation space and pixel space.

fits_no_version.finding: In ViT-B/16, the sum of the representations of images A and B resembles the representation of the combined image. This beats a calibrated baseline in representation space (p < 10^-5, N = 10) but not in pixel space (p ≈ 0.88).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision model representations of composite images are approximately additive in their parts (within-model linear superposition).

record.peer_reviewed: Nature Machine Intelligence (venue stated in metadata; the supplied text identifies itself as arXiv:2503.01824v1)
record.problems: The relevant own result is an additivity analysis within one model, not a test of cross-model convergence. The paper reports significance values but does not give a numerical effect size for the reported aggregate additivity analysis.
record.rows_left_out: No results from cited studies were included as this paper’s own results. The illustrative elephant/ball and dog/cat examples in Figure 1 do not have separately reported numerical outcomes in the text.

untested.parts: All: no measurement of cross-model alignment versus scale.
All: no models trained from different seeds compared.
All: no mapping or stitching between models; the linear identifiability theorem is cited from Reizinger et al.
All: universality of SAE features is discussed only through cited work.
All: no similarity-metric or input-dependence analysis.
All: no measurement of how complete alignment is, or of its causes.

record.verdict_notes: There is a title/version discrepancy (the arXiv 2503.01824 text versus the NMI DOI), but the document appears to be the same work. The cited contrast between Lan et al. 2024 (universal SAE feature spaces) and Paulo & Belrose 2025 (SAEs learn different features) bears on V5. It is not this study's own evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Whether alignment between independently trained models rises with model scale or capability.
Whether paired image and caption representations from vision and language models align more as both models improve.
Whether separately initialized networks of the same architecture learn shared features or subspaces.
Whether representations can be mapped between models by the mapping methods described in this version.
Whether interpretable features or circuits recur across different models.
Whether cross-model convergence varies with similarity metrics, settings or input distributions.
Whether cross-model alignment is incomplete or plateaus, and whether shared data or objectives explain it.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Tested additivity of representations for combined images against the calibrated baseline.
rows.measure: Statistical significance of additivity over the calibrated baseline, defined as the cosine similarity of the representations of A and B alone.
rows.baseline: cosine similarity of the representations of just “A” and “B”
rows.note: The paper states that the additivity finding is statistically significant in neural representation space. This measures within-model compositional additivity, not alignment across models.
rows.check: Within-model compositional additivity in one ViT-B/16 (p < 10^-5 over a baseline, N = 10); no cross-model comparison, so it bears on no version. The state 'observed' applies only to the additivity claim. It is not a convergence state.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Tested additivity of combined images in pixel space against the calibrated baseline.
rows.measure: Statistical significance of additivity over the calibrated baseline.
rows.baseline: cosine similarity of the representations of just “A” and “B”
rows.note: The paper states that the finding is not statistically significant in pixel space. This is a comparison of representation space with pixel space, not a comparison between models.
rows.check: A pixel-space comparator for the same additivity test (p ≈ 0.88); it bears on no version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
